newsitem.title: Australia: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: LANDCARE URGES RABBIT CONTROL
Landcare Australia is urging farmers and landcare groups to come up
with effective control measurers after the Rabbit Calici-virus is
released next month.
Landcare Chief Excecutive Brian Scarsbrick says the virus could wipe out about 90 percent of the estimated 300 million wild
rabbits in Australia.
He says without the effective follow-up, the long term impact on rabbit numbers could be minimal.
Mr Scarsbrick says the rabbit virus release is an opportunity for landcare groups to overcome serious environmental problems such as
loss of habitat, risks to endangered species, erosion and salinity.
He says farmers can maximise the effectiveness of the virus release
by following up with conventional control techniques like poisoning
and burrow ripping.
VANSTONE DENIES RIFT WITH UNIVERSITIES
Federal Education Minister, Amanda Vanstone, says the Coalition's
policies on higher education have come largely from university
vice-chancellors, who're now complaining.
She says some academics have taken exception to her recent comments
that university administrators are helpless, dependent and unable
to cope with change.
But Senator Vanstone says she doesn't see that there's a rift
between her office and the university vice-chancellors.
She says she stands by the comments and universities need to realise that A$680 million in funding cuts over four years is not the end of the world.
PASSENGERS HANDED CUSTOMS LEAFLETS AGAINST FUNDING CUTS
Customs officers are today trying to enlist the support of
travellers to ward off funding cuts to the Customs Service.
Australians arriving and leaving on overseas flights, importers and
people landing in Canberra on domestic flights have been handed a
leaflet.
It says the Customs Service has lost a thousand staff in the past
five years, 300 this year, while the number of tourists and imports
have increased.
The Public sector Union is asking travellers to raise the matter
with their local MPs and the Prime Minister.
AUSTRALIA-NZ DISCUSS INVESTMENT AND TAX
Australia and New Zealand have exchanged letters, setting down an
agenda for official talks on extending investment and tax aspects
of Closer Economic Relations between the two countries.
New Zealand's Finance minister Bill Birch has written to Treasurer,
Peter Costello saying while investment between the two countries has flourished, an agreement on investment could provide greater investor certainty.
On taxation, talks will centre on double taxation of shareholders'
dividends from companies resident in one country, which earn income
through a subsidiary in another country.
Mr Birch has suggested it's made clear to investors that they are examining the issues, rather than having agreed to any specific changes.
NORTHERN TERRITORY CALLS FOR END TO INTERVENTION
Northern Territory Chief Minister Shane Stone has called on all State and Territory leaders to tell the Federal Government to mind
its own business. He says a Federal Liberal backbenchers' bill to over-ride the Territory's volunatry euthanasia legislation is just one example of
the Federal Government intervening in state affairs.
Mr Stone wants the States and Territories to send a communique to the Federal Government telling it not to interfere when parliaments
properly consider and pass legislation.
He says he already has support from the ACT's Chief Minister and the Victorian Premier.
The Federal euthanasia bill is on the agenda for this week's leaders' forum in Melbourne.
QANTAS AD UPSETS ALICE SPRINGS
The Mayor of Alice Springs says Qantas has admitted it went wrong
with an advertisement for flights to the town
The Qantas Airlink ad features a picture of a zipper with the
caption, "Now you can zip down to the Alice without getting stuck there".
Mayor Andy McNeill says the advertisement is offensive and
detrimental to Alice Springs, especially when tourism numbers this
season have been down.
He says he's made an official complaint after being approached by
several people about the ad, and Qantas has assured him it won't be
repeated.
FISCHER SEEKS TO CALM CHINA ON TRADE
Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister, Tim Fischer, says no
single issue should be allowed to derail the relationship between Australia and China.
He's urged China not to carry out its threat to retaliate against Australian companies doing business in China, just because the Prime Minister is going to meet the Dalai Lama tomorrow.
Mr Fischer says the Dalai Lama is here as a spiritual leader and
Australia is committed to the One China policy.
He's told ABC Radio that Australia is committed to expanding links
with China.
Mr Fischer says while China does not not want interference in it's
internal affairs, neither does Australia.
COMMONWEALTH BANK DEFENDS CHINESE INTERESTS
The Commonwealth Bank says it's in the interests of both Australia
and China for the bank's offices in China to continue operating.
The Chinese Government has threatened to retaliate against
Australian countries doing business in China because the Prime
Minister has decided to meet Tibet's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama.
In a news article released a day ahead of the meeting, China's
Communist Party accuses Australian politicians of having ulterior
motives and interfering in China's internal affairs.
The Commonwealth Bank's Lyndell Deves says the bank is not unduly
concerned despite the renewed warning from the Chinese Government
The ANZ and insurance giant National Mutual are among other major
Australian financial institutions actively engaged in China.
CALL FOR HISTORIAN TO BE BARRED
The Ethnic Coalition of Australia says the question of allowing
controversial British historian David Irving to visit Australia is not an issue of freedom of speech.
Mr Irving says he'll reapply for a visa, citing the Prime
Minister's comments that under the Coalition Government people can now talk about certain things without being branded a bigot or racist.
Mr Irving has been barred from Australia and other countries as an
undesirable, for questioning the Holocaust and associating with
extremist and neo-Nazi elements.
Mark Liebler of the Ethnic Coalition says the Government is well
aware of the dangers of allowing a person with such a reputation
and criminal convictions into this country.
He says Mr Irving's application should be rejected.
DOWNER WARNS AGAINST PUSHING INDIA
Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer, says India will be
encouraged to sign the comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty in the
fullness of time.
Mr Downer and representatives of the five major nuclear powers have
signed the Treaty today.
The Minister says any heavy handed attempts to force India to sign
would be counter productive and create ill will in New Delhi.
India has refused to ratify the document partly because it allows
the nuclear powers to maintain their nuclear arsenals.
Mr Downer says at least 60 countries are committed to signing the treaty in the immediate future.
AIRPORT MAINTENANCE CLOSURE CONDEMNED
Union and community leaders in Geelong have condemned the closure
of the ASTAAS aircraft maintenance company, with the loss of more
than 450 jobs.
The company's board yesterday announced the immediate closure of
the plant at Avalon airport.
The Federal Government says a buyer for the firm couldn't be found
because the heavy aircraft maintenance market is depressed.
But, Geelong Trades and Labor Council secretary, John Kranz, says
the Government and the board have turned their back on Geelong and
all of Regional Australia.
He wants a meeting with the ASTAAS board this morning to find out
how hard it tried to find a buyer.
Meanwhile, Geelong's Acting Mayor Adrienne Edgar says the closure
means the loss of technology and expertise to a region with 8-and-a half per cent unemployment.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
